beats.care: If your name or a family member's vanished from the list, this drive is your chance. Check the draft list on 12 November.
beats.what: The Hindu's editorial says the Election Commission's new voter-list update is needed, but it does not fix the damage done by SIR.
beats.why: The update restarts yearly enrolment after a pause, and drops paperwork that SIR had demanded, which the paper reads as an admission.

cards.body: The paper argues the EC is now undoing parts of SIR without saying so: the old Form 6 is back without the ancestry declaration, and checks that mapped voters to older lists are gone. That, it says, shows those rules were never needed. It wants re-enrolments counted separately from new voters, house visits so people aren't burdened twice, and old 2002–03 rules for future revisions.
cards.title: A necessary corrective
cards.verdict: Bottom line: the summary revision helps, but wrongly deleted voters must be put back, and the EC must answer for SIR.

cards.body: The Hindu says the ratio fell between the 2024 Lok Sabha rolls and the SIR rolls, and young married women struck off must get a chance to re-enrol.

cards.body: A summary revision mainly adds new voters and fixes errors. It doesn't automatically bring back people removed during SIR, and the paper says the EC hasn't said what happens to lakhs of pending appeals.
cards.title: why does it say 'necessary but not sufficient'?

a.body: SIR was badly flawed, the new drive is an implicit admission, and CEC Gyanesh Kumar should resign.

b.body: Revisions keep lists accurate, and every registration officer must ensure no eligible citizen is left out.
